rationale: LFP is replacing NMC in 48V packs on cost and life, with sodium-ion next. Some NMC 48V for high-power P2 systems and legacy platforms remains, so 70 is judged.

Analysts call 800V 15-20% of BEVs by 2030, still a minority; entry and small-pack BEVs gain little from 800V because their charge power is limited by pack size, so 400V persists at the bottom. The 50% long-run plateau is judgement.

applicable segment: EV batteries placed on the EU market (BEV + PHEV)
rationale: The EU Battery Regulation (EU) 2023/1542 makes a digital passport mandatory for EV batteries placed on the EU market from 18 Feb 2027, so EU-market adoption goes to ~100%. If the segment is taken as global production, the ceiling should be cut to the share of production that reaches regulated markets (judged ~50%).
reviewer flag: Segment = batteries sold in the EU; for global production ~50.

rationale: Prismatic blade/short-blade cells dominate Chinese volume, and 46xx is a multi-OEM but minority format (BMW, Tesla, Rivian). One unattributed search result cites ~21% of the battery market for 4680 by 2030; its origin could not be verified, so the 20 is labelled judgement.
FPC/CCS is the cost-down default and wins against both round-wire harness and wireless BMS on cost. A small remainder stays on wBMS or legacy module designs, so 85 rather than 90.
Module deletion is becoming the default for new platforms; some modular packs stay for serviceability, multi-vehicle commonality and repair/insurance rules, so a ceiling of 75 is judged, not 90.

technology: Direct / hydromet battery recycling at scale
applicable segment: end-of-life EV battery tonnage processed (not vehicle fitment)
rationale: Hydromet (incl. pyro-then-hydro hybrids counted as hydromet-finished) already dominates Chinese processing, and EU recycled-content minima push the rest of the world the same way. Pure pyro and export persist for some flows, so the ceiling is a judged 70. Note: this segment is recycling throughput, not new-vehicle share.
reviewer flag: Segment is recycling throughput, not vehicle fitment.

applicable segment: Li-ion cell production capacity for EVs (process share)
rationale: This is a factory process, so the ceiling is a share of cell capacity. Yield and throughput problems (the Tesla 4680 history) and installed wet-coating lines that will not be written off early cap it; judged 40.
reviewer flag: Segment is cell-factory capacity, not vehicle fitment.

rationale: China GB 38031-2025 (effective July 2026) requires no fire/explosion after thermal runaway, and UN GTR 20 / ECE R100 propagation requirements push the same way. Cell-to-cell barriers become mandatory engineering content in practice, so the default 90 is right.

A full 1000V domain plus MW charging only pays off on flagship and performance vehicles, and only where MW chargers are built (mainly BYD/China); 800V covers the mainstream fast-charge need. The 10 is a judged figure that rests on this segment structure.

applicable segment: new BEV + PHEV traction packs (by vehicle)
rationale: LFP is already ~40% and published 2030 outlooks put it at 40-50%; it will not take the premium/long-range tier (high-Ni, LMR) and its own successors (LMFP, Na-ion entry) split the phosphate share, so ~60% is a judged plateau, not a sourced saturation figure.

LMR targets large-pack trucks and SUVs (GM, Ford) between LFP and high-Ni; voltage fade is still unresolved. Judged a niche-to-minority chemistry, aligned with the li-metal (20) and semi-solid (15) entries.

Mid-tier step between LFP and NMC; it competes for the same volume as plain LFP and ultra-fast LFP, so it is judged a significant minority chemistry rather than the default. No long-run penetration forecast found.
Pyro-disconnect plus an integrated BJB is becoming standard crash-safety content. Some entry/low-voltage designs keep a fuse and contactor without pyro, so 85.

applicable segment: end-of-life BEV/PHEV packs (share reused before recycling)
rationale: Second life competes with falling new-LFP storage cell prices and with recycling value for NMC packs; repurposing cost and liability limit it to well-graded packs. A minority channel.

Silicon-containing blends will be common, but silicon-DOMINANT anodes are forecast at only a few percent of anode supply by 2035, tied to high-nickel premium cells; LFP cells, which are growing, gain little from them. 15% is a generous judged cap.
reviewer flag: Benchmark Minerals: engineered Si only 2.9% of anode supply by 2035 — 15 may be generous.

rationale: SNE Research puts solid-state at roughly 6-13% of the secondary-cell market in 2035 (two figures reported); ceiling set slightly above to allow post-2035 growth, matched to the semi-solid entry (15). The cited figure is a dated 2035 forecast that includes non-EV cells, used as a proxy for saturation.
China has made charge speed the main spec, but 4C+ is only worth paying for where megawatt or very fast public charging exists. Many BEVs charging at home will not pay for it, so judged 40.

Chinese volume packs are staying wired because flex-PCB CCS harnesses undercut wireless on cost (see the note on this entry), so wireless is judged to stay a minority, held mainly by GM-style platforms and second-life-focused designs.
Niche-to-moderate process competing with stamping, extrusion and casting for a handful of long members; judgement.
Only mixed Al/steel (multi-material) bodies need adhesive-dominant joining; steel-intensive and gigacast-dominant BEVs use less. Ceiling approximates the multi-material BEV body share.

applicable segment: new vehicles with aluminium sheet closures/structures
rationale: Applies only where aluminium sheet is used; within that slice, scrap-tolerant alloys and CBAM make high recycled content the cost and carbon default, limited by scrap availability/segregation in regions without closed-loop press-shop return.

S&P Global's 15-20% figure is the share of BIW stampings at risk by 2030 (a dated point, not a vehicle-share ceiling); repairability, insurance write-off and capex counterforces plus the move to modular Gen-3 casting limit monolithic gigacasting to a minority-to-large share of BEV platforms. 40 is judgement anchored on that source.

applicable segment: all new light vehicles (share of vehicles with a material low-CO2 steel content)
rationale: Long-run uptake is capped by H2-DRI capacity and by China's blast-furnace-dominated production for the largest vehicle market. T&E proposes 75% green content in EU cars by 2035 but that is an advocacy target, not a forecast, so not used as a source.

applicable segment: all new light-vehicle BIW production (by paint-shop volume)
rationale: The energy and CO2 savings apply to every paint shop, but adoption follows paint-shop re-qualification and capex cycles and material cost premiums; 60% is a judged long-run share.
Mega-blank hot stamping competes with gigacasting and with conventional multi-piece floors; laser-welded blank and furnace capacity plus repairability limit it to a minority of platforms.

applicable segment: all new light vehicles (steel-bodied crash cells)
rationale: Competes with incumbent 1500/1800 MPa PHS and aluminium; gains are a few kg per part and hydrogen-embrittlement/weldability limit part selection. Expected as a minority grade on selected parts across a sizeable fraction of steel bodies.

technology: Aluminium sill/rocker crash extrusions for packs
rationale: Already the default BEV rocker answer, but 3D roll-formed/UHSS steel sills win on cost for value BEVs; judgement that aluminium keeps a majority.
CTB/CTC is spreading fast in China (BYD, Leapmotor, Tesla structural pack) but conflicts with pack reparability, second-life and multi-chemistry platform strategies in the West. Judgement.
Mature technology (B-pillars) already widespread in PHS-intensive bodies; ceiling held below universal for aluminium bodies and markets with lower PHS content.

Chinese cost-down makes CDC a mid-trim option, but base trims and A/B segments keep passive dampers. Set a little above the air-suspension ceiling (35) because semi-active is cheaper and is fitted with or without air springs.

applicable segment: all new light vehicles (global; EU Euro 7 type approvals are the hard driver)
rationale: Euro 7 brake-PM limits force a compliance answer in the EU, but coated discs compete with regen-heavy BEV strategies, rear drums, low-emission pads and brake-dust filters, and most non-EU markets have no brake-PM limit yet. 45 reflects EU near-universal pull plus partial spill-over elsewhere.
Needs EMB, steer-by-wire and in-wheel/close-coupled drive to all mature together (the in-wheel-motor ceiling is 10). Early adoption is robotaxis and LCV skateboards; judged a niche in passenger cars.

First series production arrives in 2026 (Brembo Sensify, Chinese suppliers) under the new GB 21670-2025. It needs a redundant LV supply and fail-operational design, so it competes with mature one-box EHB. No penetration forecast found; judged 30.

technology: High-output rack EPS for heavy pickups, LCVs and heavy BEVs
applicable segment: new heavy pickups, LCVs and heavy BEVs only
rationale: Within this segment, lane-keep, trailer assist and BEV conversion all need electric steering, so hydraulic recirculating-ball gear disappears over time (GM 2027 Silverado HD); the cap below 90 allows for severe-duty/chassis-cab variants. If applied to all light vehicles the ceiling would be the segment share (~10-15%).

Euro 7 regulates tyre abrasion, which is met by compound, not by sensors; in-tyre sensing is pulled by by-wire chassis and premium functions, so it saturates well below universal. Judgement, no long-run penetration forecast found.

In China EHB is fitted to more than 50% of new cars and one-box has about 87% of EHB fitments (2025). Electrification takes it toward the default, but long-run EMB substitution and low-cost ICE keeping vacuum booster + ESC cap it, so 80. The sources are current measured shares, not a long-run forecast.
Fail-operational steering is only required where the system is L2+ hands-off or L3 eyes-off (and for steer-by-wire); the ceiling equals a judged long-run share of hands-off/eyes-off-capable cars.

Published forecasts give market value in dollars, not vehicle penetration. Redundant fail-operational hardware costs and homologation keep it to premium vehicles, robotaxis and yoke-equipped vehicles for a long time, so 30 is judged.

applicable segment: ICE + PHEV vehicles with longitudinal propshafts (RWD/AWD)
rationale: Only longitudinal-driveline vehicles carry a propshaft, and the BEV shift erodes that base; within it CFRP wins where a one-piece shaft deletes a centre bearing (long-wheelbase trucks/SUVs). Cost gap keeps it a minority.

China's PHEV/EREV market already runs largely on DHTs (BYD DM-i, Geely, Great Wall) while many Western PHEVs reuse converted ATs/DCTs with a P2 motor; 48V MHEVs keep conventional gearboxes. 60 assumes DHT becomes the majority hybrid architecture but P2-in-existing-box persists for carry-over platforms.

Only multi-motor (AWD) BEVs have a secondary axle to disconnect; AWD is roughly a third of BEV volume, and the range gain makes it near-standard within that slice. The ceiling is the AWD share, not the adoption rate within it.

Any BEV can use it, but gear NVH, bearing speed limits and rotor retention cost keep a share of programmes at conventional 15-18k rpm; judgement that well over half migrate as cheap BEVs chase active-material savings.

technology: Hollow monobloc halfshafts & high-angle CV joints
rationale: Universal applicability, but hollow monobloc tooling pays back at high torque/volume; solid shafts remain cheapest on low-torque small cars. Judgement.
Requires two or more independently controlled motors; ceiling is the multi-motor share of BEVs (dual + tri/quad), assumed ~35-40% long-run. Within that slice adoption is close to universal.
3-in-1 is today's norm; deeper 6/8-in-1 integration is led by Chinese OEMs. Serviceability, supplier splits and multi-motor layouts limit it outside vertically integrated makers, so 45.
Double-sided cooling competes with single-sided direct-cooled pin-fin modules and top-side-cooled discretes, which are cheaper to assemble; it wins in high-power-density drives only.

PMSM keeps the efficiency and power-density lead, so EESM is a rare-earth hedge for some OEMs (Renault, BMW Gen6, Nissan). The ceiling depends on rare-earth geopolitics; judged 20, matching the iron-nitride magnet hedge (30) as the other route.

applicable segment: BEV + PHEV power electronics (OBC/DC-DC first, then traction)
rationale: GaN can win much of OBC/DC-DC, but traction-class GaN is unproven at TRL 6 and SiC is well established. The blended ceiling of 35 is judgement.
The entry is specifically 8-layer / X-pin / W-pin, not hairpin in general. Many cost-led motors will stay on 4-6 layer hairpin, and round wire stays in low-power P0/P2 machines, so judged 50.
This only applies to EESM motors (ceiling 20 of BEVs). If about half of EESMs go contactless, the share of all BEVs is about 10. The structure is firm; the 50% split is judgement.

technology: Motor-inverter boost charging (drive reused as DC-DC)
rationale: Only relevant to 800V BEVs that must charge on 400V DC chargers (a judged ~50% of BEVs), and of those some keep a dedicated DC-DC or pack-switching; as 800V chargers proliferate the need fades.

applicable segment: NdFeB magnet feedstock for new EV motors (recycled share)
rationale: Recycled supply is limited by the slow return of end-of-life magnets while EV magnet demand grows, so recycled share is structurally limited. The EU Critical Raw Materials Act benchmark (recycling to cover 25% of strategic raw-material consumption by 2030) is used as the anchor. This is a policy target, not a penetration forecast.

Only OEMs with very large xEV volume (Tesla, BYD, Li Auto, Geely and similar) can justify in-house module design and packaging lines; everyone else buys modules. The ceiling is the judged volume share of those OEMs.
The default for new high-power designs. Low-power secondary axles and cost-led motors keep water-jacket-only cooling, so 75.

technology: SiC power stage as volume default
rationale: SiC is effectively required at 800V and spreads down as 200mm wafers cut the price. Si IGBT keeps cost-led entry 400V and secondary axles, so judged 70. No published long-run inverter-share forecast found; the McKinsey source supports the structure only.

Silver sinter and clip bonding is a SiC-enabling package; it is limited to SiC drives (Si IGBT keeps entry and LFP 400V cars) and most SiC modules will adopt it. The ceiling equals a judged long-run SiC traction-inverter share of about 60%.

technology: Ultra-thin electrical steel & bonded lamination stacks
rationale: Rising motor speeds (higher electrical frequency) make <=0.25mm gauge and bonded stacks worthwhile in most new BEV motors. Cost-led low-speed and P0/P2 machines stay at 0.30-0.35mm, so 60.
25-30k rpm brings rotor containment, bearing and gear NVH costs that only pay back in compact performance or space-constrained drives, so judged 25.

Published 48V forecasts (e.g. ~33% of European LVs by 2030) concern 48V mild hybrids, not 12V deletion, so they do not apply. A full 12V delete requires redesigned components across the supply base; judgement that it remains a minority of BEVs.

Aluminium suits power and battery runs, and flat conductors suit zonal short links; termination and crimp reliability and the copper price cycle keep round copper in signal circuits. The ceiling counts vehicles using it meaningfully, not 100% of harness mass.

Ethernet is already in most new cars for ADAS/infotainment; a multi-gig backbone follows zonal/central compute, which is expected to dominate. Held at 85 rather than 90 because low-cost ICE carry-over platforms will keep CAN/CAN-XL backbones for years.

V2L is already standard on Korean and many Chinese BEVs and an industry coalition targets at least 30% bidirectional capability in Europe by 2030; the long-run ceiling of 70% is judgement, allowing for cost-led entry models that skip it.

applicable segment: new BEVs + PHEVs with a central computer
rationale: Chiplets pay off only at the top of the compute range and depend on automotive-qualified advanced packaging; most central computers will stay monolithic SoCs.

technology: Camera driver & occupant monitoring as standard
rationale: EU GSR2 (Reg. 2019/2144) requires drowsiness warning and advanced distraction warning on all new EU registrations (ADDW from July 2026), and NCAPs reward direct monitoring, so camera DMS approaches universal; kept below 90 because the US and some emerging markets have no mandate.

An 800V e-compressor is only fitted on 800V-architecture BEVs; 400V platforms (most LFP and entry BEVs) keep 400V compressors. The ceiling equals a judged long-run 800V platform share of about half of BEVs.

applicable segment: all new light vehicles with L2+ ADAS
rationale: End-to-end stacks are becoming the default for L2+/NOA software (China at scale), but basic regulatory ADAS (AEB, lane keep) on entry cars stays rule-based and certifiable, and validation of ML in safety cases slows uptake in some markets.

technology: Heat pump as standard BEV equipment
rationale: Heat pumps are already 55% of BEVs and are the cold-climate default; hot-climate markets and cheapest LFP city cars can keep PTC-only, so it stays just short of universal.

applicable segment: all new light vehicles (share of front/corner radar units)
rationale: Anchored on a ResearchAndMarkets forecast that 4D radars will exceed 50% (54.5%) of automotive radar by 2030. Caveat: that is a share of radar UNITS in a China-focused report, not vehicles, so confidence is low.
reviewer flag: Source figure is a share of radar UNITS in a China-focused report, not vehicles.

rationale: The cost and leak-point reduction applies to every BEV thermal loop, so it becomes the mainstream architecture; low-cost BEVs with simple loops and distributed-supplier sourcing keep a minority share.
Euro NCAP child-presence-detection points push a sensor into most cars, but CPD can also be met by cabin cameras or UWB key anchors, so dedicated 60 GHz radar will not be universal.

technology: Hands-off L2+ / conditional L3 on volume cars
rationale: Combined L2+/L3 penetration is forecast above 50% by 2035 (IDTechEx) and McKinsey sees about one in three new cars with L3+ by 2035; China L2/L2+ penetration is forecast above 90% by 2030. 60 is the long-run ceiling for hands-off/L3 specifically, below basic L2, with entry segments and regulatory variation as the cap.

Price collapse removes the cost barrier, but camera-only OEMs (Tesla and followers) and entry trims without highway NOA structurally stay lidar-free; China leads well above the global average. 40% is a judged long-run share, not a forecast.

Tesla and several BEV makers have moved to lithium 12V, but lead-acid keeps a strong cost, cold-crank and recycling case. Eurobat expects only 3% of ALL new cars to have lithium 12V by 2030. 50% of xEVs is a judged long-run cap, and some BEVs may delete the 12V battery entirely.
reviewer flag: Anchor (3% by 2030) is from Eurobat, a lead-acid industry body — possible bias.

rationale: Within North America, SAE J3400 (NACS) has been adopted by essentially every major OEM, so it approaches the whole segment; 90 is right ONLY if the segment is North-American sales. If Horizon applies the ceiling to global sales, the cap should be the NA share of xEV sales (~10-15%).
reviewer flag: Segment = North American sales only; against global sales the ceiling should be ~10-15%.

rationale: Mandated AEB (EU GSR2, US FMVSS 127 from 2029) puts the sensing in every car, which makes basic pre-crash actions cheap; full occupant positioning and reversible belt pretensioners stay premium.

Driven by the EU F-gas phase-down and the possible PFAS restriction on R1234yf; without a binding R1234yf ban outside the EU, cost and high-pressure (R744) or flammability (R290) engineering keep most programmes on R1234yf. A PFAS ban would justify raising this.
reviewer flag: Raise if the EU PFAS restriction bans R1234yf.

applicable segment: all new light vehicles (vehicles whose main MCU/SoC sourcing includes RISC-V cores)
rationale: RISC-V will win MCU and accelerator sockets (Quintauris, Infineon, Chinese sovereignty push), but Arm and TriCore keep the large installed software base; 40% is a judged share of main-compute sourcing.

UN R155/R156 mandate cybersecurity and software-update management systems, not a full SDV platform; but OTA-capable centralised software is becoming table stakes on electrified platforms. Judgement tied to the zonal ceiling.
e-fuses follow the move to zonal architectures and become the default power-distribution approach on SDV platforms; low-cost legacy architectures keep melting fuses for a long time.

Published estimates put UWB in over a third of cars by 2030 and Chinese digital-key fitment (all technologies) above 80%; the long-run 60% is judgement, since entry cars can make do with BLE/NFC keys.
Compute above 500 TOPS is needed for urban NOA/L3 end-to-end stacks; mainstream cars with highway L2 run on 100-250 TOPS chips, so about half the segment is a judged cap.
Every SDV/zonal platform consolidates functions onto an HPC with a hypervisor; legacy distributed architectures on low-cost and ICE carry-over platforms keep physical ECUs for a long time.

technology: Virtual validation & vehicle digital twins at scale
applicable segment: new vehicle programmes (development process, not fitted content)
rationale: This is a development method that every OEM with software releases adopts, and regulators (UN R157/ADS rules) accept virtual evidence. Nothing structural stops it reaching all programmes, so keep the default.
reviewer flag: A development process, not vehicle content — 90 retained.

rationale: Published forecasts are dated points, not ceilings: McKinsey ~18% of all vehicles by 2030, S&P ~40% of new vehicles by 2034, Infineon 50% of EVs by 2030. Electrified platforms lead, so 80% of new BEV/PHEV is a long-run extrapolation beyond those points; carry-over domain platforms account for the remainder.
BEV silence pulls it down-segment; mass and cost keep entry BEVs on tempered side glass. Judgement.

technology: Adaptive driving beam unlocked in the US (FMVSS 108 ADB rule)
rationale: With matrix hardware already built for Europe, enabling ADB in the US becomes a calibration cost on cars that have matrix lamps; base trims with simple LED reflectors will not get it. The share follows matrix-lamp fitment, judged at about 40%.

applicable segment: all new light vehicles (in practice only L3+ ADS-equipped vehicles in markets that permit them)
rationale: The lamp is only fitted to vehicles with an approved automated driving system (L3+), which is a low single-digit share; China has barred it on new type approvals and the UN regulation is still a draft.

technology: Aero wheel covers & low-drag wheel design
rationale: Near-zero-cost range gain, but customer styling preference for open wheels on premium/performance trims caps it. Judgement.

China's rule (new approvals from 1 Jan 2027, all designs by Jan 2029) mandates mechanical releases inside and outside and bans fully hidden electronic handles; semi-flush designs with mechanical release survive, so the ceiling sits only just above today's share. Regulation-limited.
High-resolution (16k+ pixel) modules spread down-segment on the LED cost curve but basic LED/matrix adaptive beams satisfy most needs; projection functions remain premium-to-upper-mid. Judgement.
Radar-transparent closed panels are increasingly common on BEVs; illumination is a brand-design choice. Judgement.
Slim micro-optic lamps are a styling and packaging choice that lowers depth and mass; conventional projectors stay cheaper for volume low beams, so it is a design-led minority.
Same structure as interior PCR: EU ELV recycled-content mandate makes PCR fascia/cladding grades near-universal for EU-sold vehicles, voluntary elsewhere.
reviewer flag: Treats an EU mandate as global pull.

rationale: Fixed panoramic roofs are already default on many Chinese NEVs; e-dimming is premium; hot-climate heat load and rollover/headroom packaging keep a share on metal roofs. Combined ceiling judgement.
Brand-differentiation feature; OLED lifetime/temperature and cost confine it to premium and upper-mid. Judgement.

technology: Active aero beyond shutters (flaps, diffusers, ride height)
rationale: Pays back in range-rated segments; entry BEVs keep passive aero. Aligned with the register's aero-ride-height ceiling (40), lower because it adds actuators beyond ride height.

applicable segment: all new light vehicles (tailgate body styles: SUV/hatch/estate)
rationale: Applies only to tailgate body styles (majority of volume as SUVs dominate); within those, steel/aluminium stays cheaper at very high volume. Judgement on the within-slice split.
Content feature led by Chinese NEVs and premium; cost-sensitive segments get basic ambient strips at most. Judgement.

Anchored on Frost & Sullivan's 2030 forecast of ~37% HUD penetration in Europe (~30% North America); the ceiling assumes AR/panoramic HUDs eventually replace conventional combiner/windshield HUDs, but do not spread beyond the HUD-buying population. AR-HUD is a subset of that figure, so this is an upper anchor.

UN R79/R171 require a hands-on check for lane-keeping and DCAS, and capacitive sensing removes false warnings; torque-based detection remains legal and cheapest on entry cars, and camera DMS can partly substitute.
Euro NCAP far-side protocols make it effectively necessary for a 5-star rating in Europe, and other NCAPs are following, but it is not a legal mandate and budget cars in NCAP-weak markets skip it.
Road-noise ANC needs accelerometers plus a capable audio DSP/amplifier, which entry BEVs often lack; plausible as standard on mid/premium BEVs. Judgement.
Only relevant where leather was the incumbent (premium); half of the segment assumed to keep leather as a luxury signal, especially in luxury SUVs and China/Middle-East preferences.
ELV recyclability pull is real but the mandate is on recycled content, not mono-material design; acoustic performance compromises keep mixed stacks on premium. Judgement.

Multi-display cockpits are a styling and cost choice, not a requirement; several OEMs are moving back to physical controls and smaller displays (Euro NCAP 2026 physical-control points), which caps the share.

The EU ELV regulation mandates vehicle-level post-consumer recycled plastic content, which makes PCR interior grades near-universal for EU-sold vehicles; outside the EU uptake is voluntary/OEM-target driven, hence below 90.
reviewer flag: Treats an EU mandate as global pull.

rationale: Crash re-certification and cost confine Mg/composite seat structures to BEV-packaging-driven and premium programmes; judgement aligned with zero-gravity-seats (25).

technology: Functional smart surfaces (heating, lighting, touch in trim)
rationale: Aligned with the register's in-mold-electronics ceiling (40): smart surfaces are one application of IME/printed electronics, so slightly lower.
Panel exciters and headrest audio suit premium spatial-audio and mass-saving cases; conventional cone speakers remain cheapest for mainstream sets, so it stays a minority architecture.
Voice assistants are forecast to be in nearly 90% of new vehicles and LLM back-ends are replacing command trees across them; the cap below 90 reflects unconnected entry vehicles in emerging markets.

applicable segment: new vehicles with an ICE that are not full/plug-in hybrids
rationale: In EU/China CO2 regimes 48V becomes the compliance floor on remaining ICE. Cost-sensitive emerging markets (India, LatAm, ASEAN entry cars) keep 12V start-stop, so 75 rather than 90.
Excludes 3-cylinder engines and gives little on small 4-cylinders. Concentrated on large engines (US V8 trucks, 4/6-cylinder D-segment). The structure is firm; the 35 is judgement.

applicable segment: engines in new full hybrids, PHEVs and EREVs
rationale: Dedicated hybrid engines become the default base engine for full/plug-in hybrids and EREVs, but the entry's 45%+ BTE bar is reached only by best-in-class Chinese units. Many hybrids will reuse conventional engines at around 40%, so 60.

applicable segment: new light-duty diesels in Euro 6d/7-class regulated markets
rationale: SCR+DPF is required by regulation for every diesel in the segment and is already at 90. The segment shrinks but the share stays saturated.

This is a pressure step on engines with a short remaining life. A GPF meets Euro 7 PN on its own for most programmes, so 350-500 bar rails are judged to stay a minority (premium and high-output engines).

technology: Gasoline particulate filters on every GDI
applicable segment: new GDI engines (incl. hybrids) in regulated markets
rationale: Euro 6d, China 6 and Euro 7 PN limits make GPF de facto mandatory on GDI. Already at 70; saturation near 90 is right for this segment.

applicable segment: spark-ignition ICE/hybrid engines in new vehicles
rationale: These are last-generation combustion engines with shrinking R&D budgets, and pre-chamber systems are hard to control at cold start and light load. Judged a niche for hybrid and performance engines.
Electric pumps and split cooling are near-standard on hybrids and spreading through MHEV. Low-cost ICE in emerging markets keeps the belt pump, so 70.
